Use this page to extract dispensed prescriptions for your cohort and turn them
into a variable: a first dispensing date, a user/non-user flag, or the raw
material for exposure time. You need your cohort from [Phase
10](build-study-population.qmd), and you end with an `.rds` file of
dispensings, one row per fill, that the later steps on this page reduce to one
row per person.

Prescriptions are in LMDB (Lægemiddeldatabasen). In the literature the same
data are described as the Danish National Prescription Registry, the part of
the Register of Medicinal Product Statistics that holds prescriptions filled
by individuals at community pharmacies ([Pottegård et al.
2017](https://doi.org/10.1093/ije/dyw213)). LMDB has one row per dispensed
prescription, so one person can have hundreds of rows. The two columns you
almost always use are:

- **`atc`:** the drug's ATC code (Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical
  classification), for example `"A10BA02"` for metformin.
- **`eksd`:** the dispensing date, the day the prescription was collected at
  the pharmacy. Use it as the prescription date, in the same way as
  `date_contact` in LPR (the National Patient Register).

The full column list is in [Overview of registers](register-reference.qmd#lmdb).

## What LMDB covers, and what it does not {#coverage}

LMDB starts in 1995, and the data are considered complete and valid from that
year ([Pottegård et al. 2017](https://doi.org/10.1093/ije/dyw213)). There is no
medication history before 1995, so a lookback window that reaches further back
is empty for everyone, and "no prescriptions" will look like "not a user".

LMDB only holds prescriptions dispensed at community pharmacies. The following
are therefore missing ([Pottegård et al.
2017](https://doi.org/10.1093/ije/dyw213)):

- drugs given during hospital admission;
- drugs supplied directly by hospitals or treatment centres (for example
  chemotherapy, immunosuppressants and methadone for substance use);
- drugs for certain institutionalised people (typically because of
  psychiatric illness);
- over-the-counter medicine. For a drug that can be bought both with and
  without a prescription, LMDB only shows the prescribed part.

For in-hospital medication there is a newer Hospital Medication Register
(Sygehusmedicinregisteret) with data from May 2018. Its data quality has not
yet been evaluated, and some clinical specialties are missing ([Rosenkrantz et
al. 2024](https://doi.org/10.2147/CLEP.S487838)). It is held by the Danish
Health Data Authority. What to know before using it is in [Hospital medication
(SMR)](hospital-medication.qmd).

::: {.callout-warning}
**Until 1996, a child's prescriptions were recorded under the mother, not the
child.** Prescriptions for children were issued in the mother's name until
1996, and in the child's own name after that ([Pottegård et al.
2017](https://doi.org/10.1093/ije/dyw213)). If your cohort includes children
with drug exposure in those years, filtering LMDB by the child's own `pnr`
misses those prescriptions without any error: they are in the register, but
under another person's `pnr`. The source gives no exact date in 1996, so the
cautious choice is to treat a child's dispensings as reliable from 1997.
:::

## Exposure, outcome or covariate: one extract, different date filters {#roles}

Medication can be an exposure, a covariate or an outcome. As for diagnoses
([Extract from LPR](extract-from-lpr.qmd)), you make one extract of the
dispensings, and the role is decided by where `eksd` falls relative to
`index_date`:

  | Role                                   | When                                          | What you do                                    | Page                                      |
  | -------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
  | **Exposure**                           | The date exposure starts                      | First `eksd` = the person's index date         | [Phase 10](build-study-population.qmd) |
  | **Covariate** (medication at baseline) | `eksd < index_date` (e.g. 6-12 months before) | Ever/never or a count in a window before index | [Comorbidity](comorbidity.qmd)        |
  | **Outcome** (new treatment)            | `eksd > index_date`                           | First `eksd` after index                       | [Outcomes](outcomes.qmd)              |
  | **Time-varying** (on/off treatment)    | Changes during follow-up                      | Start/stop format                              | [Time-varying](time-varying.qmd)      |

If the first dispensing defines the index date, require a period before it
with no dispensing of the drug (a washout). Otherwise people who have been on
the drug for years enter as new users. LMDB starts in 1995, so nobody has a
washout that reaches further back than that.

## Extract the dispensings for your cohort {#the-pattern}

ATC codes have no D-prefix (unlike ICD codes in LPR, see [Understand
LPR](understand-lpr.qmd#icd-codes-and-the-d-prefix)), so you match directly
on the start of the code. `read_register()` requires fastreg set up with the
path to your registers, see [Parquet and
fastreg](parquet-and-fastreg.qmd#convert-sas-to-parquet) if you did not convert
them from SAS yourself.

```r
library(fastreg) # read_register()
library(arrow) # open_dataset() - fallback without fastreg
library(dplyr)

cohort_pnrs <- unique(readRDS("path/to/full_cohort.rds")$pnr) # your cohort from Phase 10

medication_rx <- read_register("lmdb") %>% # without fastreg: open_dataset("path/to/lmdb/")
  rename_with(tolower) %>%
  semi_join(tibble(pnr = cohort_pnrs), by = "pnr", copy = TRUE) %>% # ONLY your cohort
  filter(substr(atc, 1, 5) == "A10BJ") %>% # GLP-1 analogues - filter BEFORE collect
  select(pnr, atc, eksd, vnr) %>%
  collect() # only HERE is data pulled into RAM - ALL dispensings, one row per fill

medication <- medication_rx %>%
  group_by(pnr) %>%
  arrange(eksd) %>%
  slice(1) %>%
  ungroup() # first dispensing per person

saveRDS(medication_rx, "path/to/extract_medication_rx.rds") # keep all fills: the user definition below needs them
saveRDS(medication, "path/to/extract_medication.rds")
```

`substr(atc, 1, 5) == "A10BJ"` matches the whole ATC group (all GLP-1
analogues; GLP-1 is glucagon-like peptide-1). For several groups at once, use a
regular expression as in LPR: `grepl("^A10BJ|^A10BA", atc)`. Code matching
(regex, `%in%` with a code list, `!!`) is explained in [Extract from
LPR](extract-from-lpr.qmd) and [Functions:
overview](function-guide.qmd#filter-conditions). Reducing to one row per
person is explained in [Long ↔ wide format](long-wide.qmd). Here it is
`slice(1)` for the first dispensing, but it could also be ever/never or a count
in a window (see the role table above).

## Define users: at least N dispensings within a window {#defining-users}

One dispensing is weak evidence of treatment, because some people fill a
prescription once and stop. A common definition is therefore at least two
dispensings within a window, with the onset date being the date the definition
is first met.

```r
library(dplyr) # group_by, mutate, lag, filter, summarise

# Does the person have `min_dispensings` fills inside `window_days`?
# lag() looks back to the (min_dispensings - 1)th previous fill for that person,
# so the gap between them is the span of the whole qualifying run.
flag_users <- function(data, min_dispensings = 2, window_days = 365) {
  data %>%
    arrange(pnr, eksd) %>%                       # lag() needs the rows in date order
    group_by(pnr) %>%
    mutate(
      lookback = lag(eksd, n = min_dispensings - 1),
      gap_days = as.numeric(eksd - lookback)
    ) %>%
    ungroup() %>%
    filter(!is.na(gap_days), gap_days <= window_days) %>%  # the run is short enough
    group_by(pnr) %>%
    summarise(onset_date = min(eksd), .groups = "drop")    # first date the rule is met
}

users <- flag_users(medication_rx, min_dispensings = 2, window_days = 365) # ALL fills, not the first-only table
```

::: {.callout-warning}
**Sort with `arrange()` before `lag()`.** `lag()` works on row order, not on
dates. If the rows are not sorted by person and date, `gap_days` is computed
against an arbitrary earlier row, and the result is wrong without any error.
:::

The two numbers are your choices, not standards, so write them into your
methods. One dispensing can be enough for a drug taken once; for a chronic
treatment two or more is the usual requirement.

The same definition is how medication enters a comorbidity definition: for
conditions treated largely outside hospital, LMDB catches people LPR never
sees. Whether to define a condition from diagnoses, prescriptions or both is
discussed on [Comorbidity](comorbidity.qmd#diagnoses-prescriptions-or-both).

<details>
<summary>Many ATC conditions at once: `regmorbidity::mb_extract_medication_batch()`</summary>

The recipe above is the one to keep for one drug, or a few. It opens LMDB with
`read_register()`, filters, collects, and calls `flag_users()`. Use this
fold-out only when you need many ATC conditions, each with its own "N
dispensings within a window" rule. Doing that with the recipe above scans LMDB
once per condition.

`mb_extract_medication_batch()` in
[`regmorbidity`](https://github.com/sara-schwartz/regmorbidity) puts every
condition that shares the same `(min_prescriptions, window_days)` into one
query, and only the onset rows come back to R. In the bundled code list, pain
is 4 dispensings within 365 days. The other ATC conditions are 2 within 365
days, so those are one query and pain is a second. Onset is the dispensing
that meets the rule. The package is on GitHub only and in development; it
computes no score and is not a comorbidity index.

On 26 September 2026 the 15 ATC conditions then in the bundled list (14 on the
2-within-365 rule, plus pain) matched `mb_flag_users()` on the real LMDB at
DST. Conditions have been added to the list since. The DST check covers those
15, not automatically a condition added later.

Do not use `mb_extract_diagnosis_batch()` from this page. It has not been run
on DST.

```r
# remotes::install_github("sara-schwartz/regmorbidity")
library(regmorbidity) # mb_extract_medication_batch(), mb_codelist()
library(DBI)          # dbConnect, dbExecute
library(duckdb)
library(dplyr)        # tbl, rename_with

# A dbplyr lazy table on one plain DuckDB connection, as in
# "Several registers on one DuckDB connection". This function's window
# step is written for dbplyr. duckplyr::read_parquet_duckdb() gives a
# duckplyr table, and so does read_register() from fastreg 0.14.3 on
# (the CRAN version, 0.14.1, gives a dbplyr table). The plain connection
# works whichever fastreg version you have.
con <- dbConnect(duckdb())
dbExecute(con, "CREATE VIEW lmdb AS SELECT * FROM read_parquet(
  'path/to/lmdb/**/*.parquet',
  hive_partitioning = true)")
lmdb <- tbl(con, "lmdb") %>% rename_with(tolower)

# from is required. Omitting it is an error, not "start at the beginning".
# 1997-01-01 is what the package README recommends: children's prescriptions
# were recorded under the mother until 1996 (see the warning higher up on
# this page). Pass a later date if your own study starts later.
rx <- mb_extract_medication_batch(
  lmdb,
  codes = mb_codelist(),          # or conditions = c("diabetes", "pain")
  ids = cohort_pnrs,              # the same cohort as the recipe above
  code_col = "atc",               # the full code, not atc2 or atc4
  date_col = "eksd",
  from = as.Date("1997-01-01"),
  outdir = "path/to/medication-conditions"
)
```

`code_col` has to be `atc`. The shorter columns (`atc1` to `atc4`) do not
hold the full code the list is matched against.

The result is one `.rds` per condition in `outdir`. Resume skips a
rule-batch only when every condition in that batch already has a file. If
one file in the batch is missing, the whole batch runs again and overwrites
the files that were already there.

</details>

## Which ATC column? {#atc-columns}

LMDB does not hold the ATC code once. It holds it five times, at five levels,
in five separate columns. DST's [variable list for
LMDB](https://www.dst.dk/extranet/ForskningVariabellister/LMDB%20-%20L%C3%A6gemiddeldatabasen.html)
labels them `ATC-kode detaljeret` and `ATC-niveau 1` to `ATC-niveau 4`. They are
cumulative: each level repeats the levels above it and adds its own
characters.

  | Column | ATC level | Characters | Example   | What it is              |
  | ------ | --------- | ---------- | --------- | ----------------------- |
  | `atc1` | 1         | 1          | `C`       | anatomical main group   |
  | `atc2` | 2         | 3          | `C09`     | therapeutic subgroup    |
  | `atc3` | 3         | 4          | `C09A`    | pharmacological subgroup |
  | `atc4` | 4         | 5          | `C09AA`   | chemical subgroup       |
  | `atc`  | 5         | 7          | `C09AA05` | chemical substance      |

The column names and their levels come from DST's variable list. The character
counts are not stated there; they follow from the WHO standard, where level
2 is by definition the three-character code ([WHO Collaborating Centre for Drug
Statistics Methodology](https://atcddd.fhi.no/atc/structure_and_principles/)).

::: {.callout-warning}
**A pattern longer than the column can never match, and R will not tell you.**
`atc2` holds three characters. `grepl("N02A", atc2)` compares a four-character
pattern against three-character values, so it matches nothing: zero rows, no
error, no warning. The same goes for `filter(atc2 %in% c("A10A", "A10B"))`. An
empty result looks like a finding rather than a bug, and it is easy to write up
as "no exposed patients" when the truth is that the filter could not fire.
:::

So filter on `atc`, not on the level columns. It is seven characters, it
contains every level as a prefix, and `substr(atc, 1, 3)` gives you exactly what
`atc2` holds. There is no case where a level column lets you filter something
`atc` cannot:

```r
library(dplyr) # filter, select, collect

# Ischaemic heart disease treatment, defined as organic nitrates (C01DA):
ihd <- lmdb %>%
  filter(grepl("^C01DA", atc)) %>% # the full definition, in one filter
  select(pnr, atc, eksd) %>%
  collect()
```

Use `^` to anchor the pattern at the start of the code. It costs nothing and it
is the right habit from LPR, where a code genuinely can turn up mid-string.

### Which way should you write the filter?

There are two ways to keep the codes you want, and the length of your codes
decides which one to use. ATC codes are not all the same length: `N02` is three
characters, `A10BA` is five.

  | Your code list                       | Use             | Why                                    |
  | ------------------------------------ | --------------- | -------------------------------------- |
  | All codes have the same length        | `substr()` + `%in%` | Faster, and easy to read               |
  | Codes have different lengths          | `grepl()` with `^`  | Handles any length                     |

**All codes the same length.** Cut `atc` down to that length, then check whether
the result is on your list:

```r
library(dplyr) # filter, select, collect

# Four drug groups, all three characters long
my_codes <- c("A10", "C09", "N02", "M01")

lmdb %>%
  filter(substr(atc, 1, 3) %in% !!my_codes) %>% # keep the first 3 characters, look them up
  select(pnr, atc, eksd) %>%
  collect()
```

`substr(atc, 1, 3)` means "the first three characters of `atc`". Change the `3`
to match your codes: use `1, 5` for five-character codes such as `A10BA`.

**Codes of different lengths.** One `substr()` cannot serve `N02` and `A10BA` at
the same time, because they need different cut lengths. Use `grepl()` instead,
which matches whatever you give it:

```r
lmdb %>%
  filter(grepl("^N02|^A10BA|^C09AA", atc)) %>% # ^ means "starts with", | means "or"
  select(pnr, atc, eksd) %>%
  collect()
```

::: {.callout-tip}
**In doubt? Use `grepl()`.** It works for every code length, so it is never
wrong. `substr()` + `%in%` was about twice as fast on a twenty-million-row test,
which is worth having when you fetch many drug groups at once, but a correct
slow filter beats a fast broken one.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Does it save memory to filter on `atc2` first? (No)"}
It is a reasonable thing to wonder, since `atc2` is the short column, but the
filter runs before anything is loaded: nothing reaches your memory until `collect()`, and what
lands there is the rows that survived, which are the same rows either way.
`substr(atc, 1, 3)` gives you exactly what `atc2` contains, so the two are the
same query.

There is a practical catch as well. Comorbidity definitions often need more than
three characters (`A10BA` rather than `A10`), and `atc2` cannot narrow that far.
You would filter on `atc2`, then bring in `atc` afterwards to get down to the
codes you actually wanted: two steps for a result one step gives you. And if a
code longer than three characters is compared against `atc2` on its own, it
matches nothing and returns no rows without an error, so it is worth doing in
one step on `atc`.
:::

### What the level columns are for: grouping {#atc-level-grouping}

When you want a descriptive breakdown by therapeutic subgroup, `atc2` is a
ready-made grouping column and saves you a `substr()`:

```r
read_register("lmdb") %>% # the register itself: atc2 was not selected into medication_rx
  rename_with(tolower) %>%
  count(atc2, sort = TRUE) %>% # dispensings per therapeutic subgroup
  collect()
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Check this on your own extract before you trust it"}
Two minutes, and it settles both whether the columns exist and how they are
coded:

```r
library(dplyr) # select, collect

colnames(lmdb) # do you even have atc1-atc4? Not every delivery does
lmdb %>%
  select(atc, atc1, atc2, atc3, atc4) %>%
  head(20) %>%
  collect()
```

Expect `C` / `C09` / `C09A` / `C09AA` / `C09AA05` across a row: each column
repeating the one before it. If instead you see isolated fragments (`09` in
`atc2`), every `^`-anchored pattern in this section is wrong for your delivery
and you should filter on `atc` only.

Note that `names(lmdb)` may not answer this. On a dbplyr table (what
`read_register()` from CRAN fastreg 0.14.1 returns) it gives the object's own
parts (`src`, `lazy_query`), not the table's columns, so it looks as though
the columns are missing. `colnames()` works on the DuckDB object
`read_register()` returns; if you opened LMDB with
`open_dataset()` instead, use `names(collect(head(lmdb, 0)))` - see [Phase 7, Inspect your
data](inspect-data.qmd#the-shape).
:::

`atc3` and `atc4` are not filled in for every product. Not all preparations
are classified to that depth, so do not assume the columns are complete. Count
the blanks in your own extract before you build anything on them.

## Tell products apart when they share an ATC code: `vnr` and `indo` {#same-atc-different-product}

ATC classifies by active substance, not by product or indication. Two brands
with the same substance therefore get the same ATC code and cannot be told
apart on `atc` alone. Ozempic (semaglutide, type 2 diabetes) and Wegovy
(semaglutide, weight loss) both have `A10BJ06`: filter on ATC only, and you mix
diabetes treatment with weight-loss treatment.

Two columns separate them:

- **`vnr` (varenummer):** the unique key to the actual product (package). It is
  the only reliable way to isolate one specific product. `name`/`packtext`
  hold the product text if you want to recognise it by eye.
- **`indo` (indication code):** a coded indication, not free text. The
  approved indications come with the package files the Danish Medicines Agency
  (Lægemiddelstyrelsen) sends out every 14 days ([Sundhedsdatastyrelsen, note
  on the antibiotic
  statistics](https://cdn.sundhedsdatastyrelsen.dk/sundhedsdatastyrelsen/Media/638950737327641167/Antibiotikastatistik,%20forklaring%20til%20l%C3%A6getype%20og%20indikation%20statistikken.pdf),
  PDF, Danish). The code is recorded only when the
  prescriber picks an indication from the drop-down menu in the electronic
  prescription. If the doctor types the indication as free text instead, it is
  not transferred to the register and `indo` is left blank. So it can in
  principle separate the same substance across indications, but it is often
  empty. Use `vnr` as the primary product key and `indo` as a supporting
  signal, not a clean filter.

```r
# 1. Build your own list of the varenumbers that belong to the product
#    (look them up in the medicine taxonomy - one product has several varenumbers):
ozempic_vnr <- c("xxxxxx", "yyyyyy") # placeholders - replace with your looked-up numbers

# 2. Keep only the dispensings whose vnr is on your list:
medication_rx %>%
  filter(atc == "A10BJ06") %>% # semaglutide (Ozempic AND Wegovy)
  filter(vnr %in% !!ozempic_vnr) # keep only rows with a vnr from your list
```

Keep the two names in the last line apart: `vnr` on its own is the register's
column holding the varenummer, the product's ID, just as `pnr` is the person's
ID. `ozempic_vnr` is your own R vector of the varenumbers you
looked up for Ozempic; you choose the name yourself (same pattern as the code
list in [Extracting data step by step](extraction-step-by-step.qmd)). `%in%`
keeps the rows where `vnr` is found in your list, and `!!` sends your local list
into the lazy query (explained in [Extract from LPR](extract-from-lpr.qmd)
and [Functions: overview](function-guide.qmd#filter-conditions)).

::: {.callout-note}
Which `vnr` belongs to which product depends on package and strength (one
product has several varenumbers). Look them up in the medicine taxonomy for your
exact study period rather than assuming, and document the list in your code. For
`indo`, [Harbi & Pottegård 2024](https://doi.org/10.1097/EDE.0000000000001666)
found a recorded indication code on 82% of prescriptions (about 88% corrected)
and almost 100% correct when present. Their data are from 2019 and 2020; the
authors expect more missing codes before 1 October 2017, when electronic
prescribing became mandatory. Missingness varies by drug class (about 8% missing
for systemic anti-infectives versus 28% for blood-related agents). 5.6-36% of codes are nonspecific (e.g. "for the
heart" for beta-blockers); whether a nonspecific code is usable depends on your
question. The code texts are in DST's format library on the research machine
(`indo_tekster`, see DST's [notes on
LMDB](https://www.dst.dk/extranet/ForskningVariabellister/Bemaerkning/LMDB%20-%20L%C3%A6gemiddeldatabasen.html)).
A validly recorded code does not mean the
prescriber chose the correct indication: drop-down menus make wrong choices
easy, so the code is not necessarily the clinical truth.
:::

## From dispensings to exposure time: DDD, PDC and MPR {#exposure-time}

::: {.callout-warning}
**A dispensing is not the same as intake.** `eksd` tells you the prescription
was collected at the pharmacy, not that the patient took the drug, or for how
long.
:::

For an exposure that lasts over time you need exposure windows built from the
amount dispensed, not just a count of dispensings. That covers treatment
episodes, grace periods (the gap allowed between two prescriptions before a
person counts as having stopped) and adherence measures such as PDC
(proportion of days covered: the share of follow-up time covered by medicine)
and MPR (medication possession ratio: the amount dispensed divided by the
length of the period).

The LMDB columns for the amount are `apk` (number of packages), `packsize`
(units per package) and `strnum` (the numeric strength; the unit is in
`strunit`). `volume` is the number of defined daily doses (DDD) per package
([Pottegård et al. 2017](https://doi.org/10.1093/ije/dyw213), table of
variables). The DDD is the WHO's "assumed average maintenance dose per day for
a drug used for its main indication in adults", a unit of measurement and not
necessarily the dose your patients were prescribed ([WHO Collaborating Centre
for Drug Statistics
Methodology](https://atcddd.fhi.no/ddd/definition_and_general_considera/)). So
`apk * volume` gives DDDs dispensed, which is a crude duration only if your
patients take one DDD a day. DST's variable list has `voltypecode` and
`voltypetxt` next to `volume` but no labels for them; look at the values in
your own extract before you rely on `volume`. The dosage field `doso` is
essentially empty (recorded for about 0.06% of prescriptions in the
validation by Harbi & Pottegård), so dose must be derived from the package
columns.

Ready-made tools are in [`heaven`](packages-overview.qmd): `medicinMacro()`
estimates prescription lengths and average doses from LMDB, and
`hypertensionMedication()` defines hypertension from the use of at least two
classes of antihypertensive drugs.

::: {.callout-warning}
**Exposure defined by future dispensings gives immortal time bias.** If you
require a person to fill a prescription (or two) after index to count as
exposed, then by construction they survived until that date, and the time
between index and the fill makes the exposure look protective ([immortal time
bias](dst-pitfalls.qmd#immortal-time-bias)). Start follow-up for the exposed at
the first dispensing, or treat medication as a [time-varying](time-varying.qmd)
exposure.
:::
